html:
The recruiting of Pacific Islanders, often by trickery or force, to work on plantations, above all the sugar farms of Queensland in Australia between 1863 and 1904.

Ships went to the New Hebrides (now Vanuatu), the Solomon Islands and other islands looking for labourers. Some islanders signed on willingly. Others were lured aboard with trade goods, misled about how long they would be gone, or simply kidnapped. Over the four decades tens of thousands came to Queensland, and others were taken to Fiji, Samoa and New Caledonia. Many died of disease and hard work.

Britain had banned slavery, and laws were passed to regulate the trade, but enforcement was weak. In Australia the islanders were called "Kanakas". Their labour built the Queensland sugar industry.

The end came with racial politics, not mercy. The new federal parliament's White Australia policy stopped recruiting in 1904 and ordered most islanders deported from 1906. A small community stayed, and Australian South Sea Islanders are their descendants. Fiji turned instead to Indian indentured workers.
sum: The recruiting of Pacific Islanders, often by trickery or force, to work on plantations, above all the sugar farms of Queensland in Australia between 1863 and 1904.
